etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English lowe, lohe, lāh, from Old Norse lágr (“low”), from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz (“lying, flat, situated near the ground, low”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).

Cognate with Scots laich (“low”), Low German leeg (“low, feeble, bad”), Danish lav (“low”), Icelandic lágur (“low”), West Frisian leech (“low”), North Frisian leeg, liig (“low”), Dutch laag (“low”), obsolete German läg (“low”). More at lie.

definitions.definition: Pertaining to (or, especially of a language: spoken in) in an area which is at a lesser elevation, closer to sea level (especially near the sea), than other regions.
(baseball, of a ball) Below the batter's knees.
Situated close to, or even below, the ground or another normal reference plane; not high or lofty.

quote.citation: 2012, Tyler Jo Smith, Dimitris Plantzos, A Companion to Greek Art, →ISBN:
quote.text: Narrative friezes in low relief were characteristic of Ionic architecture.

definitions.definition: Low-cut.

quote.citation: 1878, Mary Eliza Joy Haweis, The Art of Beauty, London: Chatto & Windus, page 83:
quote.text: Again, observe the unmeaningness of the low neck fashion. Our mothers wore low dresses and bare arms all day long; they knew if their shoulders and arms were beautiful they would look as well by daylight as by candlelight;  […]

quote.citation: 1917, George Amos Dorsey, Young Low, page 195:
quote.text: Why do girls wear low dresses?

definitions.definition: Of less than normal height or upward extent or growth, or of greater than normal depth or recession; below the average or normal level from which elevation is measured.

quote.citation: 1607 (edition of 1967), Edward Topsell, The history of four-footed beasts:
quote.text: It is a little low hearb  […]

quote.citation: 1795, James Cavanah Murphy, Travels in Portugal, page 15:
quote.text: The men are well-proportioned, rather low than tall, have a brown complexion, and reserved countenance.

quote.citation: 1911(?), Anthony Trollope, Framley Parsonage, page 13:
quote.text: "Now you mention her, I do remember the young lady," said Mrs. Grantly; "a dark girl, very low, and without much figure. She seemed to me to keep very  much in the background."

definitions.definition: Not high in status, esteem, or rank, dignity, or quality. (Compare vulgar.)

quote.text: Therefore they must have been common in the 16th century also among the folk first of all not as a high festival food but rather as a low festival and Sunday food, if our experience proves accurate.

quote.text: Low-Sunday, is the Sunday after Easter, and is so call'd, because it is a low Festival in Comparison of that Day whereon Christ arose from Death to Life again.

definitions.definition: Humble, meek, not haughty.

quote.citation: 1829, Thomas Watson, Discourses on Important and Interesting Subjects:
quote.text: God loves an humble soul. It is not our high birth, but our low hearts God delights in.

definitions.definition: Disparaging; assigning little value or excellence.

quote.citation: 1826, Ebenezer Erskine, The Whole Works of the Rev. Ebenezer Erskine, Sermon VII, page 103:
quote.text: The humble soul has low thoughts of his own person; as David, 'I am a worm, and no man.'

definitions.definition: Being a nadir, a bottom.

definitions.definition: Depressed in mood, dejected, sad.

quote.citation: 2016, Rick Riordan, The Hammer of Thor, page 33:
quote.text: As low as I felt, at least I didn't have Hunding's [miserable] job.

definitions.definition: (video games, roleplaying games) Having few hit points remaining; damaged.
Lacking health or vitality, strength or vivacity; feeble; weak.
Dead. (Compare lay low.)

Depleted, or nearing deletion; lacking in supply.

quote.citation: 2002, V.N. Bashkin, Robert W. Howarth, Modern Biogeochemistry, →ISBN, page 151:
quote.text: When silica is in low supply other classes of algae dominate the phytoplankton composition.

definitions.definition: Small, not high (in amount or quantity, value, force, energy, etc).

quote.text: Unfortunately, low winds were the rule over the local waters and this craft was no better, if as good, as ordinary sailboats under such conditions.

definitions.definition: (especially in biology) Simple in complexity or development.

quote.text: In the case of languages spoken by very low races, like the Puris and the Tasmanians, the difficulty of deciding such a point must be very great.

definitions.definition: (in several set phrases) Being near the equator.
(acoustics) Grave in pitch, due to being produced by relatively slow vibrations (wave oscillations); flat.
Quiet; soft; not loud.

(card games) Lesser in value than other cards, denominations, suits, etc.
(now rare) Not rich or seasoned; offering the minimum of nutritional requirements; plain, simple. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1789, John Moore, Zeluco, Valancourt, published 2008, page 173:
quote.text: The Physicians ordered a low diet, and cooling ptisans in great abundance.

definitions.definition: (of an automobile, gear, etc) Designed for a slow (or the slowest) speed.
The minimum atmospheric temperature recorded at a particular location, especially during one 24-hour period.
A low point or position, literally (as, a depth) or or figuratively (as, a nadir, a time when things are at their worst, least, minimum, etc).

quote.citation: 2020 December 2, Anthony Lambert, “Reimagining Railway Stations”, in Rail, page 38:
quote.text: During the 1960s and 1970s, when both the quality of architecture and the appreciation of historic buildings reached an all-time low, British Railways was notorious for replacing good station buildings and canopies with little more than bus shelters, usually in conjunction with de-staffing.

quote.text: He also called for the US and China to rebuild their fractured relationship, which has plunged to new lows this year, but which Guterres said was “crucial” to climate action.

definitions.definition: A period of depression; a depressed mood or situation.
(meteorology, informal) An area of low pressure; a depression.
The lowest-speed gearing of a power-transmission system, especially of an automotive vehicle.
(card games) The lowest trump, usually the deuce; the lowest trump dealt or drawn.
(slang, usually accompanied by "the") A cheap, cost-efficient, or advantageous price.
Close to the ground.
Of a pitch, at a lower frequency.

In a low mean condition; humbly; meanly.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English lough, from Old English hlōh, first and third person singular preterite of hliehhan (“to laugh”). More at laugh.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English lowen (“to low”), from Old English hlōwan (“to low, bellow, roar”), from Proto-Germanic *hlōaną (“to call, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call”).

Cognate with Dutch loeien (“to low”), Middle High German lüejen (“to roar”), dialectal Swedish lumma (“to roar”), Latin calō (“I call”), Ancient Greek καλέω (kaléō), Latin clāmō (“I shout, claim”). More at claim.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To moo.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English lowe, loghe, from Old Norse logi (“fire, flame, sword”), from Proto-Germanic *lugô (“flame, blaze”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light”).

Cognate with Icelandic logi (“flame”), Swedish låga (“flame”), Danish lue (“flame”), German Lohe (“blaze, flames”), North Frisian leag (“fire, flame”), Old English līeġ (“fire, flame, lightning”). More at leye, light.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old English hlāw, hlǣw (“burial mound”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlaiw. Obsolete by the 19th century, survives in toponymy as -low.
